implementation_notes: Python has no access control, so the realization is a naming convention plus `@property`: keep `self._courses = []` and expose `@property def courses(self) -> tuple[Course, ...]: return tuple(self._courses)`. `property()` is a data descriptor (the descriptor howto calls it 'a succinct way of building a data descriptor that triggers a function call upon access'), so the attribute has no setter unless you write one - assignment fails with AttributeError while the returned tuple is genuinely immutable. Alternatives worth knowing: return `list(self._courses)` when callers expect a list, return a `collections.abc.Sequence`-implementing read-only proxy over the live list when per-read copies are too costly, or use a `tuple` field when membership never changes. None of these is enforced by the interpreter, so the negative case belongs in the tests.
pitfalls: Returning `self._courses` from the property is the classic leak: callers append to it and the owner never notices.
A property without a setter blocks assignment but not mutation of its result - only an immutable return (tuple) or a read-only proxy prevents that.
The underscore on `_courses` is a promise, not a boundary: `person._courses.append(c)` works, so treat direct field access in reviews as a defect.
The copy is shallow: mutating a Course element is visible to everyone holding a reference.
`@dataclass(frozen=True)` freezes attributes, not the list inside them: a frozen dataclass holding a list is still mutable through the list.
